updates.name: Wayne T. Swank
updates.bio: Scientist emeritus of the USDA Forest Service Southern Research Station, trained in forest hydrology (PhD, University of Washington). His listed publications center on long-term watershed experiments at Coweeta Hydrologic Laboratory, covering streamflow and water yield after logging or forest conversion, nutrient and nitrogen export, and forest succession following clearcutting.
updates.research_interests: forest hydrology; water yield response to logging and forest-type conversion; stream chemistry and nitrogen export from forested watersheds; nutrient availability after harvest; successional dynamics after clearcutting; long-term forest watershed research at Coweeta
updates.current_affiliation: USDA Forest Service, Southern Research Station
updates.notes: Old homepage (srs.fs.usda.gov/coweeta) does not resolve. FS R&D profile (200) reads 'Wayne Swank, PhD Former Employee Scientist Emeritus Southern Research Station'; publication list includes 'Wood decomposition following clearcutting at Coweeta Hydrologic Laboratory', confirming identity. Research interests derived from listed publication titles. No ORCID found (ORCID registry search for Wayne Swank returned no records). updates.name: William J. McShea
updates.bio: Wildlife ecologist at the Smithsonian Conservation Biology Institute in Front Royal, Virginia, which he joined as a postdoctoral fellow in 1986. He began by studying how white-tailed deer shape eastern deciduous forests, later adding invasive plants and disease, and works on conserving large mammals in China and Southeast Asia. He has co-chaired the IUCN Deer Specialist Group.
updates.research_interests: wildlife management; ecology of non-game animals; mammal and bird surveys; deer conservation; citizen-science pollinator and invasive plant surveys; temperate forest dynamics; forest tree demographics; forest seed production; conservation in Southeast Asia and China; large-mammal surveys in Asia and North America; warm-season grass restoration; grassland ecology
updates.current_affiliation: Smithsonian's National Zoo and Conservation Biology Institute
updates.notes: Old homepage (nationalzoo.si.edu/scbi/staff/william-mcshea) is 404; current staff page is nationalzoo.si.edu/about/staff/william-j-mcshea (200). updates.name: William K. Lauenroth
updates.bio: Professor at the Yale School of the Environment who studies dryland ecosystems. Earlier work focused on grasslands; current projects examine grass-shrub mixtures and big sagebrush communities across western North America. He relies on simulation modeling to study plant demography, ecohydrology, production, and climate-change impacts. He previously taught at Colorado State University and the University of Wyoming.
updates.research_interests: dryland ecosystems; plant population and community ecology; ecohydrology; ecosystem ecology (above- and belowground net primary production, carbon budgets, water balance); climate change effects on plant communities; grass-woody plant resource partitioning; recruitment and demography; disturbance and livestock grazing; simulation modeling; big sagebrush ecosystems
updates.current_affiliation: Yale School of the Environment, Yale University
updates.notes: Yale profile (200) lists him as Core Faculty with the title 'Joseph F. Cullman 3rd '35 Professor' and links ORCID https://orcid.org/0000-0002-3079-4484. updates.name: William T. Peterjohn
updates.bio: Professor emeritus of biology at West Virginia University. He is a biogeochemist studying how human-driven environmental change, especially chronic acid deposition and elevated nitrogen inputs, alters forest ecosystem processes. His work covers soils, plants, and herbivores in a regenerating forest, plant nitrogen uptake and stream chemistry, nitrogen-diversity links, and tree-ring isotope records of nutrient history.
updates.research_interests: biogeochemistry; global change; nutrient cycling; forest ecosystems; soil microbiology; effects of chronic acid deposition on forests; nitrogen saturation and biological N demand; plant uptake of nitrogen forms and stream-water chemistry; nitrogen availability and tree species diversity; tree-ring isotopes as records of nutrient availability
updates.current_affiliation: Department of Biology, West Virginia University
